# Writing Voice

Instructions for writing in this person's voice. Use it for speeches and formal
letters. Read the whole file before writing; the argument and sentence rules
matter more than the ornament rules.

## 1. The spine: claim, proof, question

Every piece is an argument, and it is argued in the open, in this order:

1. State the position flatly, in the first person, before you support it. Start
   the paragraph with `I say`, `I insist`, `I hold`, `I think`, or `I add, too`.
   The claim comes first and the reason follows in the same sentence or the next.
2. Prove it with a specific: a date, a vote count, the name of a measure, a line
   read out of a document. Never rest a point on generalities when a particular
   is available. If you quote a document, quote it in full at length, set it
   apart as a display quotation, and then tell the reader what it means.
3. Close the point by throwing the question back: `And now I ask why he could not
   have left that compromise alone?` Ask a question only when you can answer it
   better than the opponent can, and answer it yourself in the next sentence,
   often in three words: `Not at all.`
4. Concede something small and true before you refute the whole: `I agree to all
   that.` — then the turn. A concession is a step in the argument, not manners.
5. Name the single point at issue and keep saying it in the same words each time
   it returns. Repeat the phrase verbatim; the repetition is the argument's
   thread.

Attribute a view to its author before you answer it, and answer the author, not
the view in the abstract: "He declared that this measure would restore
tranquillity to the country" — then show what that declaration cost.

## 2. Sentences

Two speeds, and the change of speed is the meaning.

- **Long sentences carry the reasoning.** Twenty to forty words, sometimes twice
  that, built in tiers: a qualifying opening, the assertion, a parenthetical
  qualification, then the turn after a semicolon or dash. Subordinate clauses
  stack (`that ... that ... which ...`), and the verb often waits until the end
  of its clause. Write them; do not break them up for comfort.
- **Short sentences carry the verdict.** Two to seven words, standing alone after
  the long one: `It yields nothing itself; it keeps all it has, and gets all it
  can besides.` Then something blunt: `And so it is wherever you look.` Put one
  short sentence at the hinge of every paragraph.
- Balance in pairs and threes: `peaceful, if that will suffice; by the torch, if
  required`; `by craft, intimidation, and violence`. The third term is the
  sharpest.
- Repeat the governing word of a paragraph two or three times in consecutive
  sentences, in the same position in the sentence. Repeat a whole clause to mark
  that you are returning to a point: `asking him the question again`.
- Open sentences with the plain connectors: `And`, `But`, `Again`, `Now`,
  `Indeed`, `To show`, `It is idle to contend`. Never with a rhetorical
  throat-clearing.
- Personify the abstraction. Give the thing under discussion the verbs of a
  living agent: it yields, it keeps, it gathers, it encroaches, it knocks at the
  door. Sustain that for three or four sentences, then drop it.
- Similes are a single image drawn from the ordinary world, labelled with `like`
  or `as`: `It gathers strength, like a rolling snow-ball, by its own infamy.`
  One per passage, and never extend it past its first clause.
- Qualify a prediction or a judgment of motive — `I believe`, `in my judgment`,
  `it is scarcely questioned`, `if not expressed`. Do not qualify a quotation, a
  count, an oath or a denial; there the voice is flat and unguarded: `I do know
  that there is not a word of truth in it.`
- Understate the rebuke, never overstate it: `surely that difference is not a very
  material one` lands harder than an accusation. Reserve one strong word per
  piece and put it at the end of a sentence.

## 3. Words

- Public, formal, moral vocabulary for the argument: *perpetuity, tranquillity,
  consequence, provision, sanction, inaugurate, submission, endure, accede.*
- Plain short words for the rebuke and the image: *torch, bludgeon, snow-ball,
  catspaws, props, fuss, knock.*
- Switch deliberately: an ornate word for the principle, a homely word for the
  act. Both belong in the same paragraph.
- Formal diction throughout a state paper or formal letter: `I do not`, `it is`,
  `cannot`. Contractions are a marked device for a warm, self-mocking passage
  before a crowd, where the manner drops for three sentences and is then picked
  up again. Do not sprinkle them.
- British `-our` and `-ll` spellings run through the samples: *favour, honour,
  good-humouredly, tranquillity.* Keep them.
- Archaic forms are used and should be kept: `to-day`, `for ever`, `any one` (two
  words), and the subjunctive `be` — `so that a free man be not, in any case,
  surrendered as a slave`; `if the United States be not a government proper`.
- Do not soften into abstraction: no *stakeholders, framework, leverage, utilize,
  moving forward, frankly, honestly, with that said.*
- A coined label is allowed once, for satire, named from the measure it supports,
  and needs no explanation.
- Attribute quotations guardedly when the source is not certain — `I believe it
  was Shakespeare who said` — and never dress an invented line as a quotation
  from a real person.
- Borrow a well-known phrase and treat the reader as knowing it, without citation
  and without apology.

## 4. Tone

- Earnest, and in full control of it. The heat is in the argument and in the
  choice of fact, not in the adjectives. Never complain about how hardly you have
  been treated.
- Confidence shows as plain assertion, and never as a protest that you are being
  reasonable. Write `I insist`, not `I would argue that arguably`.
- Disagreement: fix it on one issue, on one named opponent, and on the record.
  Manners stay courteous on the surface — `I find no fault with him` — while the
  charge is made and repeated. Aim censure at the authors of a mischief rather
  than at the catspaws used to carry it out.
- Denial of a charge: brief, absolute, then a comment on the custom being broken
  rather than on the man: `It used to be the fashion amongst men that when a
  charge was made, some sort of proof was brought forward to establish it, and if
  no proof was found to exist, it was dropped.` Say you want no harsh language,
  then be unyielding about the fact.
- Humour is dry, self-referential and at your own expense before a crowd: an
  absurd physical image for your own argument, an admission that you do not know
  how to meet a bad style of argument. Mock conduct and reasoning, never a
  person's appearance, family or character.
- Praise is concrete, brief, and given to opponents as well as friends: talents
  that `shone out conspicuously`; a settlement made `to the satisfaction of the
  conservative parties on both sides`. Name what was well done before what was
  done wrong.
- Reassure an alarmed reader by evidence, not sympathy: state the fear, say there
  has never been any reasonable cause for it, and point to the record.

## 5. Structure

- No headings, no subheads, no bullet points, no numbered lists. Prose paragraphs
  only — except a quoted document or resolution, which is indented as a block and
  introduced by a colon: `the resolution which I now read:--`
- Open by disposing of what need not be discussed: `I do not consider it necessary
  at present... to discuss those matters... about which there is no special
  anxiety or excitement.` Then state the ground you take.
- Open a formal letter or state paper by meeting the objection the reader is
  already making, in the reader's own words, and answering it in the first
  paragraph.
- One point per paragraph, four to eight sentences. Paragraphs run long; do not
  break them for readability.
- March forward with signposts: `I add, too`, `Again,`, `But even then`, `And now
  I ask`, `I close this part of the discussion by asking...`. A reader should
  always know which point they are on.
- Move between your ground and the opponent's by naming the contrast in one
  sentence: `I insist that this is the difference between... — that...`
- Use a deferral to show you are choosing not to over-argue: `I do not wish to
  dwell on this branch of the subject at great length at this time, but allow me
  to repeat one thing...`
- Address the audience directly once or twice a piece, and at a turning point:
  `Now, fellow-citizens,`
- Close a section on the question, not on the summary. Close a whole piece on a
  pledge, a plain resolution, or a short moral sentence — never on a restatement
  of the argument.

## 6. Punctuation and form

- The semicolon is the main joiner; use it to yoke two parallel clauses, not to
  list. Three semicolon-linked clauses in one sentence are welcome.
- The dash carries the turn or the sharpening; one per long sentence. Set a
  quoted document off with `:--`
- Commas set off the interrupting phrase on both sides, and the verb comes after
  the second comma: `equally with Adams... from the North, alike answered`. Do
  not fear a comma before `and` joining clauses.
- Parentheses for the aside that would otherwise break the sentence: `(and I find
  no fault with him)`. At most two per piece.
- Quotation marks for another's exact words, and for a phrase you are holding up
  for inspection. Italics for the one word to be struck harder — `_Yes!_`, `_for_`,
  `_against_`. Never for a whole sentence.
- Exclamation marks: one per piece, and only inside a quotation.
- Numbers: spell out counts, amounts and spans of years — `seventy-two years`,
  `the small majority of six`, `one hundred and thirty-four for to forty-two
  against`. Write calendar years in figures: `1821`, `1850`.
- No emoji, no all-caps, no more than one italicised word per sentence.

## 7. Registers

- **Public speech to a crowd**: warmest and funniest. Rhythmic, with a homely
  image, an appeal to what everyone in the room already knows, and an invective
  passage capped by a moral question.
- **Debate reply / rebuttal**: shorter sentences, more `I say` and `I insist`,
  direct address to the opponent, self-deprecating humour to show you will not
  rise to a bait, and a flat denial of any charge you mean to deny.
- **Formal state paper or formal letter**: coolest and most even. No humour, no
  crowd address. Longer sentences, more qualifiers, more evidence, explicit
  reassurance, and a closing on duty rather than on passion. For a formal letter,
  take the argumentative method of the speeches and this cooler temperature.
- Do not include audience reactions, stage directions or transcription marks in
  anything you write.

## 8. Never

- Never open with background, context, a compliment to the audience, or `I hope
  this finds you well`. Open with the matter.
- Never break an argument into bullets, lists or headed sections.
- Never hedge a fact, a count, an oath, a quotation or a denial. Keep the
  qualifiers for predictions and judgments of motive.
- Never use an exclamation mark to supply emphasis that italics and word order
  should carry.
- Never attack a person's character, family or motives at large; attack the
  argument, the act, and the record.
- Never complain of your own treatment, and never claim a virtue for yourself.
  Let the record of what you said before do that work.
- Never invent a quotation, a precedent, a date or a vote count. Where a source is
  uncertain, say so in the sentence.
- Never use the modern corporate register, or business jargon of any kind.
- Never end on a summary of what you have argued. End on the question or the
  pledge.
- Never let a paragraph carry two ideas, and never let a long sentence do two
  jobs; put the second job in a short sentence after it.

## 9. Examples

These are the writer's own words. Match the movement of the sentences, not the
subject.

> I hold that, in contemplation of universal law and of the Constitution, the
> Union of these States is perpetual. Perpetuity is implied, if not expressed, in
> the fundamental law of all national governments.

> It yields nothing itself; it keeps all it has, and gets all it can besides.
> ... It debauches even our greatest men. It gathers strength, like a rolling
> snow-ball, by its own infamy.

> In a despotism, one might not wonder to see [it] advance steadily and
> remorselessly into new dominions; but is it not wonderful, is it not even
> alarming, to see its steady advance in a land dedicated to the proposition that
> "all men are created equal"?

> Have they produced any differences? Not at all. They are the very cements of
> this Union. They don't make the house a house divided against itself. They are
> the props that hold up the house and sustain the Union.

> I wish simply to say, what I have said to him before, that he cannot know
> whether it is true or not, and I do know that there is not a word of truth in
> it. ... I don't want any harsh language indulged in...

> I close this part of the discussion on my part by asking him the question again,
> Why, when we had peace under the Missouri Compromise, could you not have let it
> alone?

> Again, if the United States be not a government proper, but an association of
> States in the nature of contract merely, can it, as a contract, be peaceably
> unmade by less than all the parties who made it?
